normalized.governing_thought: Recommendation: do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; put the cash behind the software business instead
executive_summary: Every order loses money in all the evidence we have. At the median of the 14 sites our software runs, an order loses $6.17 after site costs ($2.67 even before them). Our own Columbus pop-up lost $12.57 an order. The founders' +$2.02 needs all four main inputs better than the best site has achieved.

The market is growing, but nobody in it makes money. US quick-commerce GMV grew 41.5% a year in 2022–25, yet Zipcart (−$1.90/order) and QuickBasket (−$3.40/order) both lose money. QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities in 2025.

The plan does not fit within our cash. Holding 12 months of runway leaves $7.2M to spend; the plan needs $9.5M to month 18, and even then it reaches only contribution breakeven, not profit. At median economics, nine stores lose ~$18M a year, more than the $12.0M in the bank.

The software business is a better use of the same cash. About $0.8M a year of hires to work a 37-grocer pipeline (9 at late stage, ≈$0.86M of ARR). If 60% growth holds, our illustrative path breaks even around month 26 with ≈$4.9M still in the bank.
Parcelbird can profit from quick commerce as the software supplier, without taking on the operator's losses.

slides.title: Quick commerce is growing over 40% a year, as the founders say, but the operators in it are losing money

claims.claim: Quick commerce is growing over 40% a year
evidence: Year-on-year growth +44%, +38%, +42%; 2022–25 compound annual growth 41.5%

claims.claim: Growth is real; profit is not. The national leader loses $1.90 on each order at about $1.2B of revenue.
evidence: Zipcart (national): Revenue $1,200M; EBITDA −$310M; EBITDA margin −26%; contribution per order −$1.90
QuickBasket (regional): Revenue $210M; EBITDA −$96M; EBITDA margin −46%; contribution per order −$3.40
QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities (36%) in 2025.

claims.claim: A fast-growing market tells us nothing about whether a new, smaller entrant can make money in it.
“Nobody owns the Midwest”: the pack has no data on Midwest competitors. The regional operator's retreat suggests the gap may be about economics rather than opportunity.

slides.title: At the benchmark median, every order loses $2.67 before site costs and $6.17 after them

claims.claim: The order is underwater before rent.
evidence: Gross margin on goods (27% × $34) $9.18
Delivery fee, net +$1.99
Picking and packing −$3.10
Rider cost −$7.40
Payment and packaging −$1.30
Promotions (6% of AOV) −$2.04
Contribution before site costs −$2.67
Dark-store fixed cost −$3.50
Contribution after site costs −$6.17

claims.claim: Rider cost is the largest cost: $7.40 an order, 22% of the basket.
evidence: Rider cost = $17.75 per hour ÷ 2.4 orders per rider-hour

claims.claim: Density spreads the $1.15M fixed cost over more orders, but it cannot fix a negative variable margin. However many orders a site handles, the median order still loses $2.67.
evidence: Fixed = $1.15M ÷ (900 orders × 365 days)

claims.claim: These are not hypothetical figures: they are the median of 14 sites running Parcelbird software today.
evidence: Parcelbird briefing pack, Table 3 (median of 14 software-customer sites, 2025)

slides.title: The founders' plan turns positive only by beating the best site observed on all four main inputs at once

claims.claim: The founders' plan requires inputs beyond the evidence on all four main inputs
evidence: Average order value: median $34, best $42, plan $45 — $3 above the best site
Orders per rider-hour: 2.4, 3.0, 3.5 — above the observed range (1.9–3.0)
Orders per site per day: 900, 1,400, 1,800 — above the observed range (400–1,400)
Promotions, % of AOV: 6%, 6%, 2% — one-third of the level at every site observed

claims.claim: Contribution outcomes by case
evidence: Contribution before site costs, per order: −$2.67 / +$0.49 / +$3.77
Contribution after site costs, per order: −$6.17 / −$1.76 / +$2.02
Nine-store network, per year: −$18.2M / −$8.1M / +$11.9M

claims.claim: Even at the best of each input, an order still loses $1.76 after site costs. The founders' plan has to beat that on all four inputs together.
evidence: “Best observed” takes the best value of each input. The best order value and the best density were at different sites; no site has achieved them together.

slides.title: No single input closes the gap; the plan needs all four to move beyond anything observed

claims.claim: Any one input alone, all others at benchmark median, cannot reach breakeven within observed ranges
evidence: Average order value: needed $63, best observed $42
Orders per rider-hour: needed 14.4, best observed 3.0
Orders per site per day: Not possible², best observed 1,400
Promotions cut to zero: −$4.13, n/a
² The order loses money before site costs, so more volume cannot reach breakeven.

claims.claim: Bridge from benchmark median to founders' plan, $ per order after site costs
evidence: Benchmark median −$6.17
Rider productivity 2.4 → 3.5/hr +$2.32
Promotions 6% → 2% +$1.80
Founders' plan $2.02

claims.claim: Plan with one input set back to the evidence
evidence: Density at 1,400/day (best site) +$1.52
Promotions at 6% (every site observed) +$0.22
Riders at 2.4/hr (benchmark median) −$0.31
AOV at $34 (benchmark median) −$0.73

slides.title: Our own Columbus pop-up did worse than the benchmark median on all four operating inputs, losing $12.57 an order

claims.claim: The pop-up did worse than the benchmark median on all four operating inputs
evidence: Average order value: pop-up $31, median $34, plan $45
Promotions, % of AOV: 12%, 6%, 2%
Orders per rider-hour: 2.1, 2.4, 3.5
Orders per site per day: 280, 900, 1,800
Fixed cost per order: $6.36, $3.50, $1.75
Contribution before site costs: −$6.21, −$2.67, +$3.77
Contribution after site costs: −$12.57, −$6.17, +$2.02
Pop-up fixed cost = $650,000 a year ÷ (280 × 365)

claims.claim: To be fair to the test: it ran for six weeks on a temporary site, and orders grew 18% a week. The site was running at about 410 orders a day by week six — the bottom of the benchmark range, less than a quarter of the plan's 1,800.
evidence: Working back from 11,800 orders

claims.claim: The growth was bought with 12% promotions and a $38 acquisition cost.
The founders argue that running the software makes us better operators. The one site we ran ourselves did worse than our customers' median on all four operating inputs.

slides.title: Demand is shallower than the survey suggests, and at plan economics each customer takes over two years to pay back

claims.claim: Stated intent overstates use
evidence: 44% of 1,500 Columbus residents aged 25–39 said they would use 15-minute delivery at least weekly
22% of pop-up customers were still ordering in month three, at 3.1 orders a month (less than weekly)
$38 customer acquisition cost in the pop-up (paid social and first-order credits)

claims.claim: Each customer acquired yields about 0.68 orders a month from month three (22% × 3.1). At the plan's +$2.02, recovering $38 takes about 19 orders.
Months to recover the $38 acquisition cost
evidence: Founders' plan, before site costs: +$3.77/order — 15 months
Founders' plan, after site costs: +$2.02/order — 28 months
Benchmark median or pop-up: −$6.17 / −$12.57 per order — Never: every order adds to the loss

claims.claim: A 12-month payback would need about 51% of customers still ordering at 3.1 a month: more than twice the pop-up's 22%.

slides.title: Zipcart's one contribution-positive city shows the price: a $3.99 fee, almost no promotions and 14% fewer orders

claims.claim: Contribution turned positive, at +$0.40 an order, in its densest city in Q4 2025, following a new $3.99 service fee on every order and a cut in promotions to 1% of order value.
evidence: Order volume in that city fell 14% afterwards.
Across the whole company, Zipcart still loses $1.90 an order.

claims.claim: Pricing, not density, did the work. The precedent supports charging customers more. It does not support the founders' density-led plan.
Zipcart's fix applied to our benchmark median is still negative at the median
evidence: Benchmark median −$6.17
$3.99 service fee +$3.99
Promotions 6% → 1% +$1.70
14% fewer orders −$0.57
Benchmark with Zipcart's fix −$1.05
The 14% volume loss raises fixed cost per order from $3.50 to $4.07.

claims.claim: The same fix at the best observed inputs gives about +$3.97, but no site has achieved those inputs together. Whether a fee holds volume can be tested at a customer's site without our own capital.

slides.title: The plan breaks the 12-month runway rule even on its own numbers, and a new funding round is unlikely

claims.claim: Cash available against the plan's requirement
evidence: Cash in the bank $12.0M
Reserve for 12 months' runway at today's $0.4M/month burn −$4.8M
Available to deploy $7.2M
Plan: cash needed to month 18 $9.5M
Shortfall: $2.3M

claims.claim: If it includes today's burn: $2.5M left at month 18
evidence: That is about 5 months of runway at the plan's average burn. On even spending, the 12-month rule is broken around month 11.

claims.claim: If it is on top of today's burn: cash runs out around month 13
evidence: Combined burn of ~$0.93M a month leaves a $4.7M deficit by month 18.

claims.claim: Either way, month 18 is the plan's contribution breakeven, not company profitability, and the lead investor calls a new round “unlikely”.
This is the most generous test: once the stores open, the burn rises and so does the 12-month reserve.
evidence: At the benchmark median, the nine stores would lose ~$18M a year in steady state.

slides.title: Three further risks point the same way: rider pay rules, competing with our own customers, and a distracted core business

claims.claim: Rider pay rules: Two of our three launch cities are considering minimum pay standards for delivery workers.
evidence: Every $1 an hour on rider cost adds $0.42 to each order at benchmark productivity.
Across nine stores at median volume, that is ≈$1.2M a year for each $1 an hour.
Rider cost is already the largest cost per order.

claims.claim: Competing with our own customers: Parcelbird Now would run dark stores in the same cities as the grocers we sell software to.
evidence: Several pipeline grocers want to launch their own fast delivery, and Parcelbird would become their rival.
The 9 late-stage deals (≈$0.86M of ARR) are the most exposed.
The risk is untested: we recommend asking 2–3 customers directly before any future decision.

claims.claim: A distracted core business: The software business has 81% gross margin and 60% growth, and needs only ~$0.8M a year to scale.
evidence: Parcelbird Now would commit 79% of our cash to an operating business with thin margins.
Founders' time would move from product and sales to rents, riders and stock.
A failed launch would put the software business at risk too.

claims.claim: The founders' plan keeps rider cost at today's $17.75 an hour and does not price in either of the other two risks.
Even if the unit economics worked, Parcelbird Now would expose us to higher rider costs, strain customer relationships and pull focus from a business that already works.

slides.title: Backing the software business offers a path to profitability within current cash

claims.claim: What we already have
evidence: $4.1M ARR, growing 60% a year, at 81% gross margin.
37 grocers in the pipeline, 9 at late stage. At $96k per contract that is ≈$0.86M of late-stage ARR and ≈$3.55M if every deal closed.
Another year of 60% growth means ≈26 new contracts at $96k; the pipeline holds 37.

claims.claim: Demand that fits the product: several pipeline grocers want fast delivery from their existing stores. Our software can serve the quick-commerce trend without us running stores.
Cost: ≈$0.8M a year
evidence: 2 engineers and 2 sales hires. This raises the burn from $0.40M to ≈$0.47M a month.

claims.claim: Illustrative cash balance by month
evidence: Software-first: breakeven ~month 26, $4.9M left
Parcelbird Now, $9.5M all-in: $2.5M at month 18, still burning
Parcelbird Now, $9.5M on top: −$4.7M at month 18

claims.claim: Sensitivity: at 45% growth the software path breaks even ~month 32 with $3.1M left. Below ~35% it does not work within current cash (at 30%, cash runs out first).

slides.title: Against the board's own tests, only the software-first option passes; Parcelbird Now should wait for evidence from customer sites

claims.claim: A. Launch Parcelbird Now as proposed (9 stores, 3 cities) fails all four tests
evidence: Positive unit economics: Fails — −$6.17/order at median
Fits in cash: Fails — Needs $9.5M; $7.2M available
Path to profitability: Fails — Contribution breakeven only, at month 18
Risk to software business: Fails — High: competes with customers

claims.claim: B. Smaller own-store test (1–2 Columbus stores)

Path to profitability: Fails — Adds losses; no route to profit by itself

claims.claim: What would reopen the question
evidence: A customer site keeps positive contribution after site costs for two consecutive quarters.
A customer site adds a service fee and keeps most of its volume, which Zipcart's 14% loss did not.
Month-three retention near 51% (pop-up: 22%), which would recover the $38 acquisition cost within 12 months.
Rider minimum-pay rules in Columbus, Indianapolis and Kansas City are settled and their cost is known.

slides.title: How the numbers were built, and the judgement calls made where the briefing pack was silent

claims.claim: Contribution per order: AOV × 27% + $1.99 fee − picking − (rider cost per hour ÷ orders per rider-hour) − payment and packaging − promotions. After site costs also subtracts fixed cost ÷ (orders per day × 365).
“Best observed” combines the best value of each input across sites, which flatters the case; no single site achieved them together.
Network totals: Nine stores at steady state, 365 days a year; excludes head office, launch marketing, capex and ramp-up.
The $9.5M: The pack does not say whether it includes today's $0.4M monthly burn. Both readings are shown; the recommendation holds under either.
Runway rule: Tested at today's burn (the most favourable test for the plan). Spending is assumed even over 18 months, since the pack gives no phasing.
Pop-up exit rate: Back-solved
evidence: 11,800 orders over six weeks at 18% weekly growth puts week one at ≈1,250 orders and week six at ≈2,860 (≈410 a day).

claims.claim: Software path: Treat it as illustrative, not a forecast.
evidence: today's costs are ≈$0.68M a month ($0.28M gross profit + $0.40M burn), plus $0.07M a month for the hires
Breakeven ARR ≈$11.0M

claims.claim: Option B: A smaller own-store test was added as a middle option for comparison; the founders did not propose it.

normalized.recommendation: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; put the cash behind the software business instead. Decline the Parcelbird Now launch (nine dark stores in three cities) for 2027; approve about $0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires to scale the software business; direct management to scope a store-based fast-delivery offer for the grocers in our pipeline who want one; agree the evidence that would reopen the question, gathered from customer sites rather than from our own stores.

alternatives_considered.option: A. Launch Parcelbird Now as proposed (9 stores, 3 cities)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected: fails all four tests — −$6.17/order at median; needs $9.5M with $7.2M available; contribution breakeven only, at month 18; high risk: competes with customers.

alternatives_considered.option: B. Smaller own-store test (1–2 Columbus stores)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected: considered as a middle option (not proposed by the founders). Fails unit economics (pop-up −$12.57; small sites carry more fixed cost per order); partly fits cash (loses ≈$2.0M per store a year at median, plus $0.6M capex); fails path to profitability (adds losses; no route to profit by itself); medium risk: same conflict, smaller scale.

alternatives_considered.option: C. Software-first, with a store-based fast-delivery offer
alternatives_considered.treatment: Recommended: passes all four tests — 81% gross margin software; +$0.8M/yr, runway rule holds; illustrative breakeven ~month 26 if growth ≥ ~35%; low risk: sells into the trend.

alternatives_considered.option: Zipcart-style fix (service fee and promotion cut)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Applied to the benchmark median it is still negative (−$1.05); supports charging customers more but not the founders' density-led plan; whether a fee holds volume can be tested at a customer's site without our own capital.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Based only on the January 2027 briefing pack; no external research. The pack's figures are synthetic benchmark data.
Incumbents may define contribution per order differently from our model.
The pack has no data on Midwest competitors.
“Best observed” takes the best value of each input; no site has achieved them together, which flatters the case.
Annual figures are steady state for nine stores at 365 days, before head-office costs, launch marketing and ramp-up.
Bridge steps are applied in the order shown; changing the order changes the size of each step slightly but not the total.
Pop-up ran six weeks on a temporary site; exit rate (~410 orders a day) is back-solved from 11,800 orders at 18% weekly growth.
Payback assumes no further churn after month three, which flatters the result.
The pack does not say whether the $9.5M includes today's $0.4M monthly burn, so both readings are shown; the recommendation holds under either.
Runway rule tested at today's burn (most favourable to the plan); spending assumed even over 18 months since the pack gives no phasing.
The founders' plan keeps rider cost at today's $17.75 an hour; two of three launch cities are considering minimum pay standards.
Channel conflict is the team's judgement; the pack contains no direct customer reaction to Parcelbird Now. The risk is untested.

Software path is illustrative, not a forecast: burn = operating loss, other costs flat, growth compounds monthly. At 45% growth breakeven ~month 32 with $3.1M left; below ~35% it does not work within current cash.
next_steps: Hire the 2 engineers and 2 sales staff; prioritise the 9 late-stage grocers.
Scope a store-based fast-delivery module with 2–3 pipeline grocers.
Add site-level contribution reporting to the software, so the 14 customer sites track the reopening tests.
Bring a first read on the reopening tests to the board in Q3 2027.
Ask 2–3 customers directly about channel conflict before any future decision.
normalized.extraction_notes: The charts came through as plain text only, without images. Chart values were rebuilt by matching the labels to the numbers in the extracted text: the GMV bars on slide 3, the waterfalls on slides 4, 6 and 9, the cash chart on slide 10 and the cash-balance lines on slide 12. Pairing labels with values in the bridges on slides 6 and 9 relied on the order of the text, so some pairings may be imperfect. For the slide 9 waterfall, +$1.70 was matched to the promotions cut and −$0.57 to the 14% volume loss. The executive-summary numbering in the extracted text was jumbled, so the points are given in the order they appear. On slide 14, the grey outlining of cells outside the observed range could not be seen in the text.
